What’s the Difference Between Auxiliary Heat and Emergency Heat?

Understanding Your Heat Pump Settings This Winter

As temperatures drop here in the Tri-Cities—whether you’re in Johnson City, Kingsport, Bristol, or the surrounding areas—your HVAC system works hard to keep your home warm and cozy. If you rely on a heat pump for heating, you may have noticed settings like "Aux Heat" or "Emergency Heat" on your thermostat. But what do these terms mean, and how are they different?

At Air Comfort Services, we get this question a lot from homeowners. Let’s break it down so you can understand how your heating system works and when to use each setting.

What is AUX Heat?

Auxiliary Heat (Aux Heat) is a backup heating system that works automatically when your heat pump needs extra help to maintain your desired indoor temperature.

Here’s how it works:

  • Heat pumps pull heat from the outside air to warm your home. However, as temperatures drop below freezing (common in East Tennessee winters), your heat pump becomes less efficient.
  • When this happens, your system activates Aux Heat, which uses electric resistance heating or a gas furnace (depending on your setup) to provide additional warmth.
  • It turns on automatically—you don’t need to adjust anything on your thermostat.

? When is Aux Heat used?

  • During extremely cold weather (below 35°F).
  • If the heat pump can’t keep up with sudden temperature drops.
  • When you manually increase your thermostat setting by several degrees (this triggers Aux Heat to speed up the process).

What is EMER Heat?

Emergency Heat is a manual setting on your thermostat that bypasses the heat pump entirely and uses only the backup heat source to warm your home.

Think of Emergency Heat as a “Plan B”—it’s meant for situations when your heat pump is malfunctioning or unable to work properly.

? When should you use Emergency Heat?

  • If your heat pump has stopped working (e.g., frozen coils, a mechanical issue, or damage).
  • If there’s a major ice storm or extreme weather event that prevents the heat pump from pulling in heat.
  • If your HVAC technician advises you to switch to Emergency Heat until repairs are made.

?? Important Note: Emergency Heat can be significantly more expensive to run because it relies solely on electric resistance heating or a secondary heat source. Use this setting sparingly!

Key Differences Between Aux Heat and Emergency Heat

What Should You Do If Emergency Heat Kicks In?

If your system switches to Emergency Heat, it could signal a problem with your heat pump. Here’s what to do:

  1. Check your thermostat. Verify the setting and look for alerts.
  2. Inspect the outdoor unit. Make sure it’s not covered in ice or blocked by debris.
  3. Call a professional HVAC technician at Air Comfort Services for a thorough inspection and repair.

Keep Your Heat Pump Running Efficiently This Winter

To avoid unexpected switches to Aux Heat or Emergency Heat, follow these tips:

  • Schedule a seasonal HVAC maintenance check-up to ensure your heat pump is in top shape.
  • Replace your air filters regularly to improve airflow and efficiency.
  • Keep your thermostat settings steady—frequent adjustments can trigger Aux Heat unnecessarily.

How to Fix a Furnace That Won’t Turn On

Troubleshooting Tips for Staying Warm in the Tri-Cities

Few things are more frustrating during a cold East Tennessee winter than a furnace that won’t turn on. If your home feels as chilly as the outdoors in Johnson City, Kingsport, or Bristol, don’t panic! While some issues require professional attention, there are a few things you can check before calling in the experts at Air Comfort Services.

Let’s walk you through some troubleshooting steps to get your furnace up and running.

1. Check the Thermostat

The simplest problems often have the simplest solutions. Start here:

  • Ensure the thermostat is on “HEAT.” It’s easy to accidentally leave it in “COOL” or “OFF” mode.
  • Adjust the temperature setting. Raise the temperature a few degrees above the current room temperature.
  • Check the batteries. If your thermostat runs on batteries, dead batteries can cause it to malfunction.
  • Verify the display. If the screen is blank, your thermostat may need replacement or repair.

? Pro Tip: If you have a programmable thermostat, ensure the schedule settings are correct for heating.

2. Check the Power Source

Furnaces need power to operate, even if they’re gas-powered.

  • Inspect the circuit breaker. Go to your electrical panel and check for a tripped breaker. If it’s tripped, reset it by flipping the switch to “OFF” and then back to “ON.”
  • Look for the furnace switch. There’s often a switch near the furnace (it may look like a light switch) that can accidentally get turned off.

? Safety First: If the breaker trips again, don’t keep resetting it. This could indicate an electrical issue—call a professional.

3. Check the Furnace Filter

A clogged or dirty air filter can restrict airflow, causing your furnace to shut down as a safety measure.

  • Inspect your air filter. If it’s dirty or covered in dust, replace it with a clean filter.
  • Make it a habit: Replace your filter every 1-3 months during the winter season.

? Why it matters: A clean filter improves airflow, efficiency, and the overall health of your HVAC system.

4. Inspect the Pilot Light (for Older Furnaces)

If you have an older gas furnace, a pilot light that’s out will prevent the furnace from working.

  • Look for the pilot light. It’s usually located near the bottom of the furnace.
  • Relight it if needed. Follow the instructions on your furnace or in the owner’s manual.

?? Important: If you smell gas, DO NOT relight the pilot light. Leave your home immediately and call your gas company.

5. Check the Furnace Safety Switch

Most furnaces have a safety switch on the access panel that prevents the furnace from running when the panel is removed.

  • Make sure the panel is securely closed. If it’s loose or not in place, the furnace won’t operate.

6. Look for a Fault Code

Modern furnaces have a small LED light that flashes error codes to indicate issues.

  • Find the light: It’s usually on the control board inside the furnace panel.
  • Check the code: Refer to your owner’s manual to interpret the flashes.

If you can’t resolve the issue based on the fault code, it’s time to call an HVAC professional.

7. Check the Gas Supply

If your furnace uses natural gas or propane, ensure the gas valve is open and the supply isn’t interrupted.

  • Verify the gas valve: It should be in the “ON” position.
  • Inspect other gas appliances: If they’re also not working, the issue may be with the gas supply.

When to Call the Professionals

If you’ve checked everything and your furnace still won’t turn on, it’s time to bring in the experts at Air Comfort Services. Furnace problems can stem from:

  • A faulty igniter or flame sensor.
  • Blower motor issues.
  • A malfunctioning limit switch or control board.

Attempting DIY repairs on these components can be risky and may cause further damage. Leave it to the pros!

item.title: Signs Your HVAC has Frozen Coils
item.dc:creator: masonfalkner22
item.content:encoded:
Top Signs To Look For If You ThinkYour HVAC Coils Are Frozen

How to Spot and Fix the Problem Before It Gets Worse

During the cold winters and humid summers in the Tri-Cities—from Johnson City to Kingsport and Bristol—your HVAC system works hard to keep your home comfortable. However, if your system isn’t performing as it should, you might be dealing with frozen coils.

Frozen HVAC coils are a common problem, and if left unchecked, they can lead to bigger issues like poor airflow, higher energy bills, and even system damage. In this blog, Air Comfort Services will walk you through the signs of frozen coils, what causes them, and when to call for professional help.

What Are HVAC Coils?

Your HVAC system has two types of coils:

  1. Evaporator Coils – Located inside your indoor unit, these absorb heat from your home.
  2. Condenser Coils – Located in the outdoor unit, these release the heat outside.

When the evaporator coils freeze, your HVAC system can’t circulate air effectively, leaving your home uncomfortable and potentially damaging the unit.

Signs of Frozen HVAC Coils

1. Reduced Airflow or Warm Air Coming from Vents

If you notice weak airflow or that your HVAC system is blowing warm air instead of cool air (in summer), frozen coils could be the culprit. When the coils are covered in ice, they can’t cool the air effectively.

? Quick Check: Hold your hand over a vent—if there’s little to no air coming out, frozen coils could be restricting airflow.

2. Visible Ice or Frost on the Coils or Refrigerant Lines

One of the most obvious signs is visible ice buildup on the indoor unit or refrigerant lines. Check your HVAC system:

  • Look for frost or ice on the evaporator coils (inside your air handler).
  • Check for ice on the copper refrigerant lines leading to the outdoor unit.

? Warning: Don’t try to chip away the ice—it can damage the coils.

3. Water Leaks or Pooling Around the Unit

As the ice on the coils begins to melt, it can overflow the drain pan and cause water to leak around the indoor unit. If you see water pooling on the floor, it’s a strong indicator of frozen coils.

4. Higher Energy Bills

Frozen coils force your HVAC system to work harder to maintain your desired temperature. This strain can lead to longer run times and increased energy usage, which you’ll notice on your utility bills.

5. HVAC System Frequently Turns On and Off (Short Cycling)

If your HVAC system is short cycling—turning on and off more frequently than usual—it could be struggling due to frozen coils. This issue not only makes your home uncomfortable but can also damage the compressor over time.

What Causes Frozen HVAC Coils?

Understanding the root causes can help prevent frozen coils in the future:

  1. Dirty Air Filters
    Clogged air filters restrict airflow, causing the coils to get too cold and freeze.
  • Solution: Replace your filters regularly—every 1-3 months.
  1. Low Refrigerant Levels
    Low refrigerant causes the coils to drop in temperature and freeze. This is often due to a refrigerant leak, which needs professional repair.
  2. Blocked or Closed Vents
    Closing too many vents or having blocked vents can restrict airflow, leading to frozen coils.
  • Solution: Keep vents open and clear of furniture or debris.
  1. Dirty Coils
    Dust and debris buildup on the evaporator coils can prevent proper heat transfer, causing the coils to freeze.
  • Solution: Schedule regular HVAC maintenance to keep your system clean.
  1. Thermostat or Fan Issues
    If your fan isn’t running properly or your thermostat isn’t cycling the system correctly, it can contribute to freezing.

How to Fix Frozen Coils

If you suspect frozen coils, here’s what you can do:

  1. Turn Off the System. Shut off your HVAC unit to prevent further damage and let the ice thaw.
  2. Check the Air Filter. Replace it if it’s dirty or clogged.
  3. Ensure Vents Are Open. Make sure airflow isn’t restricted by blocked or closed vents.
  4. Call a Professional. If the coils are still frozen after thawing, or if you suspect low refrigerant or mechanical issues, call the experts at Air Comfort Services.

Prevent Frozen Coils with Regular Maintenance

The best way to prevent frozen coils is through regular HVAC maintenance. At Air Comfort Services, we offer comprehensive tune-ups to ensure your system is running efficiently year-round.

? Benefits of Regular Maintenance:

  • Improved system efficiency and performance
  • Lower energy bills
  • Fewer unexpected breakdowns
  • Longer system lifespan

Call Air Comfort Services for Frozen Coil Repairs

If you suspect frozen HVAC coils in your Tri-Cities home, don’t wait—let our team at Air Comfort Services help! With over 20 years of experience serving Johnson City, Kingsport, Bristol, and surrounding areas, we’re your trusted HVAC experts for repairs, maintenance, and new installations.

? Call us today at (423) 677-7856 or schedule an appointment online!

Don’t let frozen coils leave you in the cold—trust Air Comfort Services to keep your home comfortable year-round!

item.dc:creator: masonfalkner22

Heat Pump vs. Furnace: Which Is Right for Your Home?

When it comes to heating your home, choosing the right system can make all the difference in comfort, efficiency, and cost. Two popular options homeowners consider are heat pumps and furnaces. But which one is best for your home? Let’s break down the differences, benefits, and factors to help you make an informed decision.

How Heat Pumps Work

A heat pump is a versatile system that provides both heating and cooling. It works by transferring heat from the outside air (even in cold temperatures) into your home during winter, and reversing the process in the summer to act as an air conditioner. Heat pumps are powered by electricity and are known for their energy efficiency.

Advantages of Heat Pumps:

  • Energy Efficiency: Heat pumps use less energy compared to traditional heating systems, potentially lowering utility bills.
  • Year-Round Comfort: Since they double as an air conditioner, there’s no need for a separate cooling system.
  • Environmentally Friendly: By using electricity instead of burning fossil fuels, heat pumps reduce your carbon footprint.

Drawbacks of Heat Pumps:

  • Effectiveness in Extreme Cold: Heat pumps may struggle to extract enough heat in regions with consistently freezing temperatures.
  • Higher Upfront Cost: Installation can be more expensive compared to furnaces.

How Furnaces Work

Furnaces are dedicated heating systems that burn natural gas, propane, or oil, or use electricity to produce heat. The heat is distributed throughout your home via ductwork. Furnaces are particularly effective in providing consistent warmth, even in extremely cold climates.

Advantages of Furnaces:

  • Reliable Heating in Cold Climates: Furnaces can generate significant heat, making them ideal for freezing temperatures.
  • Long Lifespan: Furnaces typically last 15-20 years with proper maintenance.
  • Lower Installation Cost: Generally, furnaces are more affordable to install compared to heat pumps.

Drawbacks of Furnaces:

  • Higher Energy Bills: Gas and oil furnaces can lead to higher operating costs depending on fuel prices.
  • No Cooling Capability: Furnaces only provide heating, so a separate system is required for air conditioning.
  • Environmental Impact: Gas and oil furnaces produce greenhouse gases.

Factors to Consider When Choosing

  1. Climate:
    • If you live in a mild or moderate climate, a heat pump may be the more efficient choice.
    • For areas with harsh winters, a furnace might be more reliable.
  2. Energy Costs:
    • Compare local electricity, natural gas, and oil prices to determine which system will be more cost-effective over time.
  3. Upfront vs. Long-Term Costs:
    • While heat pumps can be pricier to install, they often save money on energy bills in the long run.
    • Furnaces are less expensive initially but may result in higher operational costs depending on fuel prices.
  4. Environmental Impact:
    • If reducing your carbon footprint is a priority, a heat pump is the greener option.
  5. Existing Systems:
    • If your home already has ductwork in place, it may influence your decision. For example, a furnace might integrate seamlessly with your current system.

Combining Both: A Hybrid Solution

In some cases, homeowners opt for a hybrid system that combines a heat pump and a furnace. This setup allows you to use the heat pump for mild weather and the furnace for extreme cold, maximizing efficiency and comfort year-round.

At Air Comfort Services, we’ve been helping homeowners in the Tri-Cities area make smart heating and cooling decisions for over 20 years. Our experienced team can assess your home’s needs, explain your options, and ensure you get the system that’s perfect for your comfort and budget.

item.dc:creator: masonfalkner22

How to Seal Air Leaks in Your Home to Improve Efficiency

Air leaks in your home can have a significant impact on your comfort and energy bills. Drafty windows, doors, and hidden gaps let conditioned air escape, forcing your HVAC system to work harder and costing you money. Sealing air leaks is one of the most cost-effective ways to improve energy efficiency and maintain a comfortable living environment. Here’s how you can do it.

1. Identify Problem Areas

The first step in sealing air leaks is finding them. Common places for leaks include:

  • Windows and doors: Check for drafts around the edges and seals.
  • Attic and basement: Inspect where walls meet the ceiling and floor, as well as any penetrations for pipes or vents.
  • Electrical outlets and switches: Air can escape through gaps in the walls.
  • Ductwork: Look for disconnected or poorly sealed joints.
  • Fireplaces: Check the damper and surrounding masonry for leaks.

To locate leaks:

  • Perform a visual inspection for cracks and gaps.
  • Use a lit incense stick or a smoke pen to detect drafts. Move it slowly around potential problem areas and watch for movement in the smoke.
  • Consider hiring a professional for an energy audit, which may include a blower door test to identify hidden leaks.

2. Use the Right Materials

Once you’ve identified the leaks, choose the appropriate materials to seal them:

  • Caulk: Ideal for sealing small gaps around windows, doors, and baseboards. Use silicone-based caulk for areas exposed to moisture.
  • Weatherstripping: Great for movable parts like doors and windows. Self-adhesive foam strips, felt, or rubber gaskets can fill gaps effectively.
  • Spray foam: Expanding foam is excellent for sealing larger gaps and cracks, especially in attics and basements.
  • Door sweeps: Attach these to the bottom of exterior doors to block drafts.
  • Outlet gaskets: Foam gaskets can be placed behind electrical outlet and switch plates to reduce air leakage.

3. Seal Doors and Windows

  • Apply weatherstripping: Ensure a snug fit when sealing windows and doors to block drafts.
  • Caulk gaps: Use caulk to fill any gaps where the frame meets the wall.
  • Install storm doors or windows: Adding an extra layer can significantly reduce air infiltration.

4. Insulate the Attic and Basement

  • Seal attic penetrations: Look for areas where plumbing, electrical lines, or chimneys pass through and seal them with spray foam or caulk.
  • Insulate attic access points: Weatherstrip and insulate attic doors, hatches, or pull-down stairs.
  • Close gaps in the basement: Use caulk or foam to seal cracks around the foundation and sill plate.

5. Don’t Forget the Ductwork

Leaky ducts can lose up to 30% of the air your HVAC system produces. Seal ducts with:

  • Metal tape or mastic sealant: Avoid duct tape, as it doesn’t hold up over time.
  • Insulation: Wrap ducts in unconditioned spaces with insulation to prevent energy loss.

6. Maintain Proper Ventilation

While sealing air leaks improves efficiency, it’s essential to maintain healthy indoor air quality. Ensure your home has adequate ventilation by:

  • Installing exhaust fans in kitchens and bathrooms.
  • Considering an energy recovery ventilator (ERV) or heat recovery ventilator (HRV) to exchange stale indoor air with fresh outdoor air efficiently.

Benefits of Sealing Air Leaks

  • Lower energy bills: Reduce heating and cooling costs by keeping conditioned air inside your home.
  • Increased comfort: Eliminate drafts and maintain a consistent indoor temperature.
  • Extended HVAC lifespan: A more efficient system works less, reducing wear and tear.
  • Better indoor air quality: Keep out allergens, dust, and pollutants from outdoor air.

item.dc:creator: masonfalkner22
item.content:encoded:
When Should You Use Emergency Heat? ?

As temperatures drop, you may notice an "Emergency Heat" setting on your thermostat. But when should you actually use it? At Air Comfort Services, we want to help you stay warm without unnecessary costs. Let’s break it down! ?

?? What is Emergency Heat?

Emergency heat (or "auxiliary heat") is a backup heating source that kicks in when your heat pump can’t efficiently pull warmth from the outside air. It usually involves electric resistance heating, gas, or oil, which can be much more expensive to run than your standard heat pump. ??

Many homeowners mistakenly believe that switching on emergency heat will warm their home faster. However, this setting is not designed for regular use and should only be activated when absolutely necessary. Using it incorrectly can cause your energy bills to skyrocket and put unnecessary strain on your HVAC system. Understanding when and why to use emergency heat can help keep your home comfortable without breaking the bank.

? When Should You Use Emergency Heat?

? Your Heat Pump is Malfunctioning
If your heat pump isn’t working due to a mechanical failure, emergency heat will keep your home warm until a professional can fix it. ??

? Extreme Cold Weather (Rarely in Tennessee!)
In below 20°F temps, your heat pump may struggle to keep up. If your home isn’t staying warm, you may need to switch to emergency heat temporarily. ???

? Ice Buildup on Your Outdoor Unit
If your heat pump’s outdoor unit is covered in ice and won’t defrost, emergency heat can step in while you schedule a service call. ???

? Power Outages Affecting Your Heat Pump
Sometimes, power surges or temporary outages can impact your heat pump’s efficiency. If your heat pump isn’t recovering after a power outage, emergency heat may be necessary while troubleshooting the issue.

? When NOT to Use Emergency Heat

? As a Regular Heating Source – Emergency heat is for short-term use only. Running it constantly will skyrocketyour energy bills! ??

? Just Because It’s Cold – Your heat pump is designed for cold weather! Unless it completely fails, emergency heat is unnecessary. ???

? Without Checking for Issues First – Before switching to emergency heat, check for tripped breakers, airflow restrictions, or dirty filters first. ??

? If Your Heat Pump is Functioning Properly – If your heat pump is running but struggling to keep up, resist the temptation to switch to emergency heat. Instead, consider other ways to retain heat in your home, like sealing drafts, closing unused rooms, and layering up.

? How to Reduce the Need for Emergency Heat

To avoid relying on emergency heat, follow these energy-saving tips:

?? Schedule Regular Maintenance – Routine tune-ups ensure your heat pump runs at peak efficiency. Our technicians can identify potential problems before they become costly repairs. ??

?? Improve Home Insulation – Proper insulation reduces heat loss and helps your HVAC system maintain a steady temperature, even in colder weather.

?? Use a Programmable Thermostat – Setting your thermostat to an optimal temperature range prevents excessive strain on your heat pump. Keeping it at 68°F in winter can balance comfort and efficiency. ??

?? Keep Your Air Filters Clean – Dirty filters restrict airflow, making your heat pump work harder. Change your filters regularly to ensure smooth operation.

?? Check for Drafts – Seal any gaps around windows and doors to prevent cold air from seeping in and forcing your heat pump to work overtime.

? What to Do if You Need Emergency Heat

When to Call an HVAC Professional & When to Troubleshoot Yourself ?

Your HVAC system is essential to keeping your home comfortable year-round, but when something goes wrong, should you call a professional right away or try to fix it yourself? At Air Comfort Services, we’re here to help you decide! Let’s break it down. ?

? When to Troubleshoot Yourself

Before picking up the phone, check for these common HVAC issues that you can fix yourself:

? Thermostat Issues

  • Ensure it’s set to the right mode (heat/cool) and temperature.
  • Replace the batteries if your thermostat is unresponsive.
  • Check if the display is showing any error messages.

? Clogged Air Filters

  • A dirty air filter can restrict airflow, making your system work harder.
  • Change your filter every 1-3 months to keep air flowing smoothly. ??

? Tripped Circuit Breaker

  • If your HVAC unit isn’t turning on, check your breaker box.
  • Reset any tripped breakers and see if that solves the issue. ?

? Blocked Vents & Registers

  • Make sure furniture or curtains aren’t blocking airflow.
  • Keep vents open for proper circulation. ???

? Outdoor Unit Obstructions

  • Leaves, dirt, and debris can block your outdoor unit.
  • Gently clear away any obstructions for better performance. ?

? Strange Noises or Odors

  • Some noises (like mild rattling) may be due to loose screws—tighten them if safe to do so.
  • Musty smells? Check your air filter and clean any accumulated dust.

? When to Call an HVAC Professional

Some HVAC problems require expert help to prevent further damage and costly repairs. Call Air Comfort Services if you experience:

? No Airflow or Weak Airflow

  • If your system is running but air isn’t coming out of the vents, there may be a deeper issue, like a faulty blower motor. ??

? Frequent Cycling

  • If your system turns on and off constantly, it could indicate a thermostat issue, clogged filter, or electrical problem.

? Unusual Sounds

  • Loud banging, screeching, or grinding noises are signs of mechanical failure. Call for service immediately! ??

? Refrigerant Leaks

  • If you notice hissing sounds or warm air blowing instead of cold, your AC may have a refrigerant leak, which requires professional repair. ??

? Water Leaks Around the Unit

  • Puddles of water near your HVAC system may mean a clogged condensate drain or other internal issue.

? Burning or Electrical Smells

  • If you detect a burning odor or sudden electrical smell, shut off your system and call an HVAC technician immediately. ???

? High Energy Bills Without Explanation

  • A sudden increase in your utility bill may mean your HVAC system is struggling. A professional can diagnose efficiency issues and recommend solutions. ??

? Keeping Your HVAC System in Top Shape

To prevent issues before they start: ?? Schedule Regular Maintenance – Routine check-ups keep your system running efficiently and catch minor problems before they become major repairs. ?? Upgrade to a Smart Thermostat – Smart thermostats optimize energy use and alert you to potential problems. ?? Know When to Call the Pros – If troubleshooting doesn’t solve the problem, don’t wait—call the experts at Air Comfort Services! ?

? Need HVAC Help? Contact Air Comfort Services Today!

Whether you need a repair, maintenance, or a system upgrade, we’ve got you covered. Give us a call, and our expert technicians will get your HVAC system running like new! ????

?? The Importance of Changing Your HVAC Filters ??

Your HVAC system works hard to keep your home comfortable, but without proper maintenance, it won’t perform at its best. One of the simplest and most effective ways to ensure efficiency and air quality is by regularly changing your HVAC filters. Let’s dive into why this small task makes a big difference! ????

? Why Changing Your HVAC Filters is Essential

? Improves Air Quality

  • Your filter traps dust, pollen, pet dander, and other airborne pollutants. A clogged filter lets these particles circulate in your home, leading to allergies and poor indoor air quality. ???

? Boosts Energy Efficiency

  • A dirty filter makes your system work harder to push air through, increasing energy consumption and utility bills. Replacing your filter can lower energy costs by up to 15%! ??

? Extends the Life of Your HVAC System

  • Dust and debris can cause wear and tear on your system, leading to breakdowns and costly repairs. Changing your filter regularly helps keep your HVAC running smoothly and efficiently for years to come. ???

? Prevents Costly Repairs

  • A neglected filter can cause airflow problems, overheating, or even frozen coils. These issues often lead to expensive emergency repairs that could have been avoided with simple maintenance. ??

? Keeps Your Home Comfortable

  • A clean filter helps your system maintain consistent airflow and temperature control, ensuring your home stays cozy in the winter and cool in the summer. ???

? How Often Should You Change Your HVAC Filter?

  • Every 1-3 months – for most homes ?
  • Every month – if you have pets ??
  • Every 1-2 months – if you suffer from allergies ?
  • More frequently – during peak heating/cooling seasons ??

To Repair or Replace Your HVAC? Let’s Break It Down! ????

So, your HVAC system is acting up ?. You’re probably thinking, “Should I fix it or just bite the bullet and get a new one?” Don’t stress—we’ve got you covered! Here’s a super simple rule to help make the decision: If the repair costs more than 50% of a new system, it’s usually time to replace it. Let’s dive into when fixing it makes sense—and when it’s better to swap it out for a shiny new model! ?

When to Repair: Quick Fixes and Minor Problems ??

Sometimes, a repair is the way to go! Here’s when:

  • It’s a simple fix: A clogged filter or a funky thermostat? Quick and cheap! You’re good to go. ?
  • Your system is still young: If your HVAC unit is under 10 years old and hasn’t been causing too much trouble, a repair could be just what it needs to keep humming along. ?
  • You’re trying to save cash: If the repair is small and won’t break the bank, it might make more sense to fix it and keep going. ?

When to Replace: Time for a Fresh Start ?

But if your HVAC system is a little… seasoned ?, here’s when it might be time to say goodbye and upgrade:

  • It’s always breaking down: If your system feels like it's always in the shop ??, it’s probably time for a new one. ?
  • Repairs are getting expensive: If the cost of repairs is more than 50% of a new system ?, it's usually smarter to replace it (plus, a new system will save you in energy costs! ?).
  • It’s a power hog: Older systems are less energy-efficient, meaning they guzzle more energy and skyrocket your utility bills ?. A new, energy-efficient system will keep you comfy without the sticker shock. ?

What to Think About When Replacing Your HVAC ?

If you’re leaning toward replacement, here’s what you need to know:

  • Energy efficiency: Newer HVAC systems are WAY more energy-efficient, which means you’ll spend less on those pesky utility bills ?. Look for a high SEER (Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio) to get the best bang for your buck. ?

  • Get it installed right: A shiny new system is only as good as its installation. Be sure to call in the pros (that’s us! ?) to make sure everything is set up for maximum efficiency and longevity. ?

Bottom Line: Repair or Replace? ?

If your HVAC system is still in decent shape and the repair is small, fixing it might be the way to go. But if it’s costing you more than half the price of a new system ?—or if it’s just not running like it used to ?—replacement could be the best choice. ?

? Spring Into Comfort with Air Comfort Services!

Spring is here! The birds are chirping, the flowers are blooming, and the weather is just right—not too hot, not too cold. But before you get too comfortable, summer is right around the corner and your HVAC system needs a little spring TLC to keep you cool when the heatwave hits.

Use this spring checklist to prepare your AC for summer and keep your home comfortable all season long!

1. Give Your HVAC System a Spring Cleaning ?

Spring cleaning isn’t just for your closets—your AC needs it too! After sitting idle all winter, it’s time to clear out the dust and debris so your system can work efficiently.

? What to do:
?? Change your air filter (every 1-3 months for better airflow!)
?? Dust & vacuum around your vents
?? Wipe down your thermostat (dust buildup can affect accuracy)

A clean system = better air quality, lower energy bills, and a happier AC unit!

2. Clean Up Around Your Outdoor Unit ?

Your outdoor AC unit has been hanging out in the cold all winter—give it a little attention before summer kicks in!

? Spring To-Do List:
?? Clear away leaves, twigs, and dirt
?? Trim back bushes & grass (keep at least 2 feet of space)
?? Hose it down to remove dust buildup

Keeping it clean helps your system breathe easier and prevents overheating in the summer!

3. Test Your AC NOW—Before It’s 90°! ?

Don't wait for the first scorching day to realize your AC isn't working! Turn it on now and check for any issues.

? What to look for:
? Weak airflow? Your ducts might be clogged.
? Strange noises? Could be a loose part.
? Weird smells? Time for a professional check-up.

If something seems off, schedule a service call now before the summer rush!

4. Upgrade to a Smart Thermostat ?

Spring is the perfect time to upgrade your thermostat before your AC is running 24/7.

Why?
? Saves money—adjusts automatically to your schedule!
? Remote control—cool your house from your phone!
? Increased efficiency—keeps your AC from overworking.

A smart home is a cool home—literally! ?

5. Seal Up Drafts & Leaks ?

Even the best AC system won’t help if cool air is escaping! Spring is the time to seal up leaks and insulate before summer.

? Easy Fixes:
?? Check for drafts around windows & doors
?? Seal leaky ductwork (up to 30% of cool air can escape!)
?? Add weather stripping to keep cool air in!

A little effort now = lower energy bills and better cooling later! 

6. Schedule Your Spring HVAC Tune-Up ???

Just like your car needs a tune-up, your AC needs one too—before the summer heatwave arrives!

? What we check:
?? Refrigerant levels (low coolant = weak cooling!)
?? Electrical components (prevent surprise breakdowns!)
?? Coil cleaning (better efficiency, lower bills!)

? Book your AC check-up today—before everyone else does!

Spring Into Action: Get Your HVAC Ready for Summer!?

Spring isn’t just about cleaning and gardening—it’s the best time to prep your HVAC system for a stress-free, cool summer!

? Call Air Comfort Services today to book your tune-up!

Don’t wait for summer to find out your AC isn’t ready—get ahead now and stay cool all season long!

item.title: Cool for the Summer: 7 Easy Ways to Cut Your Cooling Costs & Stay Comfortable
item.dc:creator: masonfalkner22
item.content:encoded:
How to Save Money on Cooling Costs This Summer ?

Summer in East Tennessee means blazing heat, sky-high humidity, and AC units working overtime. While your air conditioner is your best friend in the heat, it can also be your wallet’s worst enemy if it’s running inefficiently.

The good news? You don’t have to choose between staying cool and saving money! Follow these simple tips to cut down on cooling costs while keeping your home comfortable all summer long. ??

1. Use Your Thermostat the Smart Way ??

Your thermostat settings can make or break your energy bill. Here’s how to use it wisely:

? Set it to 78°F when you're home for the best balance of comfort & efficiency.
? Raise it by 7-10°F when you’re away to save up to 10% on cooling costs!
? Invest in a smart thermostat—it adjusts automatically & saves $$$ on energy bills!

? Bonus: Control the temp from your phone so you’re never cooling an empty house!

2. Keep Your Air Filters Clean ???

A dirty air filter = higher energy bills because your AC has to work harder to push air through all that dust and gunk.

? Fix it in seconds:
?? Check your filter every month
?? Replace it at least every 3 months (more often if you have pets or allergies!)

Clean filters = better airflow, lower energy use, and a healthier home! 

3. Block Out the Sun ???

The sun heats up your home like an oven—and your AC has to work extra hard to fight it off.

?? Keep it cool with these easy tricks:
?? Close blinds & curtains during peak sunlight hours (especially south-facing windows!)
?? Use blackout or thermal curtains to keep heat out
?? Add UV-blocking window films for even more energy savings

Keeping the sun out = less work for your AC & more money in your pocket! 

4. Use Fans to Help Your AC Work Less ?

Fans don’t cool the air, but they help you feel cooler by moving air around. This lets you raise your thermostat a few degrees without feeling the difference!

? Best ways to use fans:
?? Ceiling fans: Run them counterclockwise to push cool air down
?? Box & oscillating fans: Keep air moving in hot rooms
?? Bathroom & kitchen fans: Use them to suck out hot air while cooking or showering

Pro Tip: Turn off fans when you leave the room—they cool people, not spaces!

5. Seal Up Air Leaks & Insulate! ??

If cool air is escaping, your AC has to work harder and longer to keep up. That means higher energy bills!

?? DIY fixes to keep the cool air in:
?? Seal gaps around doors & windows with weather stripping
?? Check for leaks in ductwork & use duct tape or mastic sealant
?? Insulate your attic & walls to keep your home cooler longer

Less air loss = lower energy bills & a happier AC unit!

6. Limit Heat Inside Your Home ??

Your AC already works hard—don’t make it fight against extra heat!

? Simple ways to reduce heat inside:
?? Cook outside (grilling > oven heat)
?? Run appliances like dishwashers & dryers at night
?? Switch to LED light bulbs (they give off less heat & use less energy!)

Little changes = BIG savings on your cooling bill! 

7. Get a Professional AC Tune-Up ????

Your AC works best when it’s in top shape—and a quick tune-up can save you hundreds in energy costs over the summer!

? A professional HVAC check-up includes:
?? Cleaning & inspecting coils for efficiency
?? Checking refrigerant levels (low levels = weak cooling & higher bills!)
?? Ensuring all parts are working before the summer heat kicks in

? Book your AC maintenance now & avoid mid-summer breakdowns

? Stay Cool & Save Money with Air Comfort Services!

You don’t have to suffer through sky-high energy bills to stay comfortable this summer! With a few simple changes, you can save money & keep your home cool all season long.

? Call Air Comfort Services today to book your tune-up!

Let’s make sure your AC is running at peak efficiency—so you stay cool & stress-free this summer!

item.title: Is Your Home Too Humid? How to Tell If You Need a Dehumidifier
item.dc:creator: masonfalkner22
item.content:encoded:
Do You Need a Dehumidifier? Signs Your Home Has Too Much Moisture ??

Excess humidity in your home isn’t just uncomfortable—it can lead to mold growth, damage to your belongings, and even health issues. If your home constantly feels damp or sticky, a dehumidifier might be the solution. But how do you know if you really need one? Here are the key signs that your home has too much moisture and how a dehumidifier can help.

1. Your Home Feels Damp or Muggy ??

If the air in your home feels heavy and sticky, even when the air conditioner is running, excess humidity is likely the culprit. This often happens in basements, bathrooms, and other areas with poor ventilation. A dehumidifier helps remove excess moisture, making your home feel more comfortable.

2. You See Condensation on Windows or Walls ??

Noticing water droplets forming on your windows, mirrors, or walls? That’s a sign that humidity levels are too high. Over time, this moisture can lead to mold growth and even structural damage to your home.

3. Musty Odors Linger in Certain Areas ?

A musty smell is often a sign of mold or mildew growth, which thrives in damp environments. If you notice an unpleasant odor in certain rooms—especially basements, attics, or closets—a dehumidifier can help by reducing moisture and preventing mold from spreading.

4. Mold or Mildew Spots Are Appearing ??

Dark spots on walls, ceilings, or around windows are signs of mold and mildew growth. This can be harmful to your health, especially for those with allergies or respiratory conditions. Controlling humidity levels with a dehumidifier can help prevent further mold issues.

5. You’re Constantly Battling Dust Mites and Allergies ?

High humidity creates the perfect environment for dust mites, which can trigger allergies and asthma symptoms. If you or your family members are experiencing frequent sneezing, coughing, or itchy eyes indoors, reducing humidity levels can help improve indoor air quality.

6. Wood Furniture and Floors Are Warping ?

Excess moisture can cause wood floors, doors, and furniture to swell or warp over time. If you’ve noticed changes in your hardwood floors or trouble closing doors properly, high humidity could be to blame. A dehumidifier helps protect your home and belongings from long-term damage.

7. Clothes and Towels Take Forever to Dry ?

If your laundry feels damp long after it’s been washed and dried, or if towels in the bathroom never seem to dry completely, humidity levels may be too high. A dehumidifier can speed up drying times and prevent that stale, damp smell from developing.

How a Dehumidifier Helps ?

A dehumidifier works by pulling moisture from the air, reducing humidity levels, and helping your HVAC system work more efficiently. Some benefits include:

  • Improved comfort by eliminating the muggy feeling in your home
  • Better indoor air quality by reducing allergens like dust mites and mold spores
  • Protection for your home’s structure and furniture from moisture damage
  • Lower energy costs since your air conditioner won’t have to work as hard

Do You Need a Whole-Home or Portable Dehumidifier? ?

If you’re experiencing moisture issues in just one or two rooms, a portable dehumidifier may be enough. But if your entire home feels humid, a whole-home dehumidifier, installed as part of your HVAC system, might be the best long-term solution.

When Should You Schedule HVAC Maintenance?

Choosing the Right HVAC System: Heat Pump vs. Furnace vs. Central AC

When it comes to heating and cooling your home, choosing the right HVAC system is crucial for comfort, efficiency, and long-term savings. But with so many options available, how do you decide between a heat pump, furnace, or central AC system? Let’s break down the pros, cons, and best uses for each system to help you make the right choice.

Heat Pump vs. Furnace vs. Central AC: What’s the Difference?

Each system has a unique way of keeping your home comfortable. Here’s a quick overview:

  • Heat Pumps – Provide both heating and cooling by transferring heat instead of generating it.
  • Furnaces – Use gas or electricity to produce heat, making them ideal for colder climates.
  • Central AC – Cools your home efficiently but requires a separate heating system.

Now, let’s dive deeper into each option.

Heat Pumps

Best for: Moderate climates with mild winters.

How It Works

A heat pump moves heat rather than generating it. In the summer, it extracts heat from your home and releases it outside, just like an air conditioner. In the winter, it pulls heat from the outdoor air (even in cold temperatures) and transfers it inside to warm your home.

Pros:

? Energy-efficient – Uses less energy than traditional heating methods.
? All-in-one system – Provides both heating and cooling.
? Lower operating costs – Reduces reliance on gas or oil.

Cons:

? Less effective in extreme cold – May need a backup heating source in freezing climates.
? Higher upfront cost – Installation can be pricier than other options.

Furnaces

Best for: Cold climates where temperatures drop below freezing.

How It Works

A furnace generates heat using gas, oil, or electricity. It then distributes the warm air throughout your home using ductwork.

Pros:

? Powerful heating – Works well even in freezing temperatures.
? Long lifespan – Can last 15-20 years with proper maintenance.
? Quick heating – Warms your home faster than a heat pump.

Cons:

? Heating only – Requires a separate cooling system, like central AC.
? Higher energy costs – Gas or oil can be expensive in some areas.
? Carbon monoxide risk – Gas furnaces require proper ventilation for safety.

Central AC

Best for: Homes that already have a furnace or another heating source.

How It Works

A central air conditioner cools your home by removing heat and humidity from the indoor air and releasing it outside. It uses ductwork to distribute cool air evenly throughout your home.

Pros:

? Consistent cooling – Cools the entire home evenly.
? Long-lasting – Typically lasts 10-15 years with routine maintenance.
? Increases home value – A central AC system is a great selling point.

Cons:

? Cooling only – Requires a separate heating system, like a furnace or heat pump.
? Higher energy usage – Can be costly if not properly maintained.
? Requires ductwork – Not ideal for homes without existing ducts.

Which HVAC System Is Right for You?

Here’s a quick guide to help you decide:

  • Choose a heat pump if… you want an energy-efficient, all-in-one heating and cooling solution in a mild climate.
  • Choose a furnace if… you live in an area with harsh winters and need a powerful heating system.
  • Choose a central AC if… you already have a heating system and need reliable whole-home cooling.

DIY HVAC Maintenance: What You Can Do & When to Call a Pro

Regular HVAC maintenance is essential for keeping your system running efficiently, preventing costly breakdowns, and extending its lifespan. While some maintenance tasks can be handled on your own, others require the expertise of a professional.

So, what can you do yourself, and when is it time to call the pros? Let’s break it down!

DIY HVAC Maintenance Tasks

These simple maintenance steps can help keep your system in top shape and prevent common issues:

1. Change Your Air Filters Regularly

? How Often? Every 1-3 months, depending on pet dander, allergies, and usage.
? Why? Dirty filters restrict airflow, reducing efficiency and indoor air quality.
? How? Locate the filter slot, remove the old filter, and insert a new one with the airflow arrows pointing in the correct direction.

2. Keep Vents & Registers Clean

? How Often? Once a month.
? Why? Blocked vents make your system work harder, increasing energy costs.
? How? Use a vacuum to remove dust and debris from vents and make sure furniture isn’t blocking airflow.

3. Check & Clean the Outdoor Unit

? How Often? At least twice a year (spring and fall).
? Why? Leaves, dirt, and debris can block airflow and reduce efficiency.
? How? Turn off the power, remove any debris around the unit, and gently rinse the coils with a garden hose (never use a pressure washer).

4. Adjust Your Thermostat for the Season

? Why? Optimizing your thermostat settings can save you money on energy bills.
? Recommended Settings:

  • Summer: Set to 78°F when home, 85°F when away.
  • Winter: Set to 68°F when home, 60°F when away.

5. Inspect & Clean Drain Lines

? How Often? Every few months.
? Why? Clogged drain lines can cause water leaks and mold growth.
? How? Pour a cup of vinegar down the drain line to help clear buildup.

When to Call a Professional

Some HVAC issues require a trained technician. Here’s when you should leave it to the pros:

1. Strange Noises or Odors

? Signs: Loud banging, screeching, rattling, or a burning smell.
? Possible Issues: Loose parts, electrical problems, or motor failure.

2. Weak Airflow or No Cooling/Heating

? Signs: Some rooms feel warmer or cooler than others, or the system isn’t reaching the set temperature.
? Possible Issues: Refrigerant leaks, ductwork blockages, or compressor failure.

3. High Energy Bills Without Explanation

? Signs: Sudden spikes in energy costs without changing usage habits.
? Possible Issues: Dirty coils, duct leaks, or an aging system struggling to keep up.

4. Frequent Cycling On & Off

? Signs: The system turns on and off too frequently.
? Possible Issues: A faulty thermostat, dirty filters, or an issue with the compressor.

5. Ice Buildup on Your AC Unit

? Signs: Ice forming on the indoor or outdoor coils.
? Possible Issues: Low refrigerant, poor airflow, or a dirty evaporator coil.

A broken furnace in the middle of a freezing Tri-Cities night, or an AC that won’t cool during a sweltering summer, can turn a bad day into a serious emergency. Knowing how to recognize an HVAC emergency, what you can do in the moment, and when to call a professional can make all the difference.

At Air Comfort Services, we’ve helped Johnson City, Kingsport, and Bristol homeowners stay safe and comfortable for over 20 years. 

Here’s what every homeowner should know about handling an HVAC emergency the smart way.

What Counts as an HVAC Emergency?

Not every HVAC hiccup is a crisis, but certain issues should never be ignored. 

Recognizing the warning signs can save you from costly repairs, prevent damage to your home, and keep your family safe.

No Heat During Freezing Weather

When your furnace fails during a Tri-Cities cold snap, your home can quickly become uncomfortable and unsafe, with risks like frozen pipes.

Before calling for help, try these quick checks:

  • Make sure your thermostat is set to “heat” and has working batteries.
  • Inspect your circuit breaker for a tripped switch.
  • Confirm your furnace’s air filter isn’t completely clogged.

If it still won’t start, the issue could be a blown fuse, bad ignition switch, or faulty blower motor, which are all issues best handled by a professional.

Our team provides 24/7 heating repair throughout the Tri-Cities and can restore your home’s warmth quickly and safely.

AC Failure During Extreme Heat

Tri-Cities summers get hot and humid, and a broken AC can quickly become a health risk for kids, pets, and older adults.

Here’s what to check before calling for service:

  • Make sure your thermostat is set to “cool.”
  • Check and replace your air filter if it’s dirty.
  • Ensure your outdoor condenser unit isn’t blocked by debris.

If it’s still not cooling, you may have low refrigerant, frozen coils, or a failing compressor. Turn off your system and call for emergency AC repair to prevent further damage.

Air Comfort Services will quickly find the problem and get your system cooling again, or recommend an energy-efficient replacement that lowers your monthly bills.

Burning or Electrical Smells

A burning or electrical odor from your vents or HVAC unit is never a good sign. This could mean overheating motors, frayed wires, or failing components—all potential fire hazards.

A light burning smell when you first turn on the heat in winter can be normal as dust burns off. But if it’s strong, smoky, or comes with sparks, take action:

  1. Turn off your system immediately
  2. Don’t try to restart it
  3. Call a professional right away

Our certified technicians will inspect and repair your system safely, with up-front pricing and a one-year service warranty, so you can rest easy knowing your home is protected.

Strange Noises or Vibrations

Your HVAC system should run quietly in the background, not make you jump every time it turns on.

Listen for these warning sounds:

  • Banging or clanging: Loose or broken parts in the blower or motor
  • Grinding or squealing: Worn-out bearings or belts
  • Rattling: Loose panels, ductwork, or debris inside the unit

Ignoring these sounds can turn a small issue into a costly repair, or even full system replacement. Shut off your unit and call for professional HVAC repair before the problem escalates.

Air Comfort Services technicians use diagnostic tools to identify exactly what’s causing the noise, fix it fast, and get your system running quietly and efficiently again.

Gas or Carbon Monoxide Concerns

Gas leaks and CO exposure are serious HVAC emergencies. If you smell gas (like sulfur or rotten eggs) or your CO detector sounds, leave immediately and call emergency services.

Once it’s safe, our licensed HVAC pros can find and fix the cause, such as a cracked heat exchanger, blocked vent, or faulty gas valve.

Prevent problems with annual furnace maintenance and working CO detectors. If your system is older, consider upgrading to a sealed combustion furnace for added safety.

What You Can Safely Do Before the Pros Arrive

While waiting for a technician, you can take a few safe steps to protect your system and your home:

  1. Check your thermostat and breaker – Dead batteries or a tripped switch are common culprits.
  2. Replace your air filter – A clean filter helps your system breathe and may restore temporary function.
  3. Turn off the unit if it smells or sounds strange – Prevent fire or mechanical damage.
  4. Avoid DIY fixes – Modern HVAC systems are complex; quick “YouTube” repairs can make things worse or void warranties.

When It’s Time to Call for Emergency HVAC Repair

When you reach out to Air Comfort Services, here’s what you can expect every time:

  • Honest recommendations on whether repair or replacement makes the most sense.

With over 40 years of combined experience, our team has seen (and fixed it all, from frozen heat pumps to failed compressors.

Stay Comfortable—No Matter What

Quick Answer:

If your heater is blowing cold air, the most common culprits include incorrect thermostat settings, a clogged air filter, ignition issues, blocked vents, or an overheating furnace. Cold air blasting from your vents on a chilly Tennessee morning is never a good sign. But don’t worry—many heating issues are simple to diagnose, and in some cases, you can fix them yourself.

Below, we break down the most common reasons your furnace or heat pump might be blowing cold air, what to check first, and when it’s time to call a professional.

1. Your Furnace Needs a Minute to Warm Up

When your heating system first turns on, it may push out some cool air. That’s normal—it’s clearing out the cold air sitting in the ductwork.

Quick Fix: Give the system a few minutes to warm up. 

If it doesn’t, there’s no need to panic. It just means it’s time to dig a little deeper with a few simple checks to find out what’s really going on.

2. Your Thermostat Settings Are Off

Before assuming the worst, check your thermostat settings. If your fan is set to ON instead of AUTO, it’ll keep blowing air even when your furnace isn’t producing heat, making it feel like your system is failing.

Quick Fixes:

  • Switch thermostat to HEAT, not COOL
  • Set fan to AUTO
  • Replace old or weak thermostat batteries

Small adjustments like these can make a big difference in how your system performs.

3. Your Air Filter Is Dirty

A dirty or clogged air filter can make it harder for air to flow through your heating system, which can make your home feel colder than it should.

Quick Fix: Change your filter every 30–90 days. Homes with pets, dust, or allergy concerns may need more frequent changes.

Regular filter replacements also help reduce breakdowns and lower energy bills.

4. Pilot Light or Ignition Problems

Gas furnaces may stop producing heat when the pilot light goes out or the electronic igniter fails.

Quick Fix: Check if the pilot light is on. If it’s out, you can relight it only if you’re comfortable and know the procedure.

Safety Warning: If you smell gas, turn off the system, leave the home, and call us for emergency service immediately.

Our licensed technicians handle all gas-related repairs safely and quickly.

5. Your Furnace Is Overheating

Restricted airflow, often caused by dirty filters, closed vents, or ductwork issues, can trigger your furnace’s safety shutoff. The burner turns off, but the blower keeps running, sending cool air through your home.

Quick Fix: Make sure every vent is fully open and clear of furniture, rugs, or other obstructions so air can circulate properly throughout your home.

If the furnace continues overheating, schedule a professional inspection. Repeated overheating can lead to major problems that are costly to fix.

6. Heat Pumps Naturally Blow Cooler Air

Heat pumps are common throughout the Tri-Cities, and they heat differently than gas furnaces.
Because they move heat rather than generate it, the air from your vents may feel cooler, even when it’s effectively heating your home.

Quick Fix: If the air feels cold (not just cool), Air Comfort Services can check refrigerant levels, reversing valves, and defrost cycles.

7. Your System Needs a Professional Repair

1. Dress in Layers and Use Extra Bedding

Staying warm starts with layering your clothing and bedding:

  • Wear sweaters, thermal socks, and hats, even indoors, to prevent heat loss.
  • Add extra blankets or a sleeping bag at night to trap body heat.
  • Keep emergency blankets or portable warming packs handy for unexpected cold snaps.

These small steps help maintain warmth while our team works to restore your heating system.

2. Block Drafts and Limit Heat Loss

Even a fully functional heater can’t combat drafts. 

During an outage:

  • Close doors to rooms you aren’t using.

  • Cover windows with thick curtains or blankets.
  • Keep fireplace dampers closed when not in use.

A few simple adjustments can keep your main living spaces noticeably warmer.

3. Use Safe Alternative Heating Options

If your heating system is out, there are other ways to heat your home safely. 

Safe options:

  • Electric space heaters with tip-over protection and auto shut-off, positioned at least 3 feet from flammable items.
  • Gas or wood fireplaces, ensuring flues are open and operational.
  • Monitored electric blankets for temporary warmth.

Avoid:

  • Heating with ovens, stovetops, or outdoor grills indoors.
  • Fuel-burning heaters without proper ventilation.

Only use devices designed for indoor heating to avoid fire hazards and carbon monoxide poisoning.

4. Keep Moving to Generate Heat

Physical activity increases circulation and helps your body stay warm:

  • Walk around your home or do light household chores.
  • Stretch or perform short exercise sessions every 20–30 minutes.
  • Play with kids or pets to keep everyone moving.

Even moderate activity can significantly improve warmth in a cold house.

5. Warm Up From the Inside Out

Eating and drinking warm items helps your body maintain heat:

  • Drink hot tea, cocoa, or coffee.
  • Eat soups, stews, or other warm meals to sustain energy.
  • Avoid alcohol, which can temporarily feel warming but lowers core body temperature.

Internal heat works hand-in-hand with layers and blankets to keep you comfortable.

6. Monitor Vulnerable Household Members

Children, seniors, and those with medical conditions are more prone to cold stress:

  • Ensure they have multiple clothing layers, warm socks, and hats.
  • Keep them in heated rooms with access to warm beverages.
  • If indoor temperatures drop dangerously low, consider relocating to a friend, family member, or local warming center.

Safety is always the top priority during a heating emergency.

7. Know When to Call an Emergency HVAC Technician

Some heating problems shouldn’t wait.

  • Repeated system cycling or breaker trips

item.title: Furnace Safety Checks Tri-Cities Homeowners Should Do Before Holiday Guests Arrive
item.dc:creator: astafford
item.content:encoded:
When cold weather settles into the Tri-Cities and the holidays bring people in and out of your home, your furnace has a lot more work to do. Before guests arrive, a quick safety check can protect your home from unexpected breakdowns, and make sure your space stays warm and comfortable.

Air Comfort Services has been serving Johnson City, Kingsport, and Bristol for over 20 years, with technicians who bring 40+ years of combined experience. Our team knows exactly how holiday stress, cold snaps, and constant stop-and-go heating cycles can expose problems fast.

Use this simple checklist to make sure your home is ready.

1. Inspect and Replace Your Furnace Filter

A clogged filter restricts airflow and makes your furnace work harder than it needs to, especially when doors are opening constantly and more people are indoors.

What to do:

  • Remove the filter and hold it up to a light. If you can’t see through it, replace it.
  • Most homes need a fresh filter every 1–3 months.
  • Consider upgrading to a high-efficiency filter for cleaner indoor air during holiday gatherings.

Why it matters: Better airflow = better comfort, better efficiency, and fewer furnace issues during busy holiday weeks.

2. Test Your Thermostat

Even small thermostat issues can create hot-and-cold spots or cause your furnace to run nonstop.

What to do:

  • Switch your system to heat and slowly raise the temperature.
  • Make sure your furnace responds quickly and maintains a steady temp.
  • If you have a programmable or smart thermostat, double-check your holiday schedule settings.

Pro tip: A responsive thermostat reduces energy waste and keeps your home consistently warm for guests.

3. Check Airflow, Vents & Visible Ductwork

Blocked vents and leaky ducts are common causes of uneven heating in Tri-Cities homes.

What to do:

  • Walk room to room and check that warm air is flowing normally from every vent.
  • Move furniture, luggage, boxes, and holiday decorations away from vents.
  • Look at any accessible ductwork for loose sections or obvious gaps.

Call Air Comfort Services if you notice weak airflow, unusual odors, or cold rooms that never warm up.

4. Listen and Smell for Warning Signs

Your furnace will often give subtle clues before a real problem develops. Paying attention to unusual sounds or odors can help you catch issues early.

Noises to watch for:

  • Rattling: Loose panels or parts.
  • Squealing: Worn belts or blower motor issues.
  • Grinding: Internal components wearing down.
  • Banging: Possible ignition or ductwork problems.

Odors that matter:

  • Burning smells (lasting more than a few minutes): Dust buildup or overheating.
  • Chemical odors: Potential electrical or component issues.
  • Gas smells: Always a serious warning.

Important: If you detect a gas smell, leave immediately and contact emergency services.

5. Test Carbon Monoxide Detectors

When a gas furnace malfunctions, it can create carbon monoxide, a colorless, scentless gas that poses serious risks.

What to do:

  • Make sure detectors are installed on every level and near bedrooms.
  • Press the test button and replace batteries if needed.
  • Replace detectors every 5–7 years or per manufacturer instructions.

Tip: Never ignore a CO alarm. Treat it as an emergency until proven otherwise.

6. Schedule Professional Furnace Maintenance

DIY checks help, but a full furnace safety inspection should always be handled by a trained technician.

A professional tune-up includes:

  • Cleaning and inspecting burners
  • Checking electrical connections
  • Testing safety switches
  • Inspecting gas lines
  • Lubricating moving parts
  • Verifying airflow and system efficiency

Why it matters: A pre-holiday tune-up dramatically lowers the risk of furnace failure when your home is full.

7. Prepare for Higher Heating Demand

If your furnace is older or has been showing signs of strain, holiday gatherings can push it over the edge.

What to do:

  • If your furnace is 12–15+ years old, schedule an evaluation.
  • Make sure the system can handle long run times and fluctuating temperatures.
  • Upgrading to a newer, energy-efficient system often delivers noticeable savings in cold Tri-Cities winters.

item.title: Heart-Warming Chocolate Lava Cake Recipe
item.dc:creator: astafford
item.content:encoded:
Valentine’s Day is all about warmth—warm hearts, cozy nights, and the kind of comfort that makes winter feel a little more romantic. At Air Comfort Services, keeping your home warm and dependable through the coldest days of the year is always the goal.

While your heating system works behind the scenes to keep your space comfortable, this Heart-Warming Chocolate Lava Cake brings that same cozy feeling to the kitchen. Rich, indulgent, and best enjoyed straight from the oven, it’s the perfect reminder that when the heat is right, everything feels better.

Whether you’re planning a quiet night in, sharing dessert with someone special, or treating yourself after a long winter day, this recipe proves that comfort starts at home—and a little extra warmth goes a long way.

Prep Time:
15 minutes
Cook Time:
12–14 minutes
Total Time:
30 minutes
Servings:
4 individual cakes
Skill Level:
Easy
Best Enjoyed:
Fresh & warm

Ingredients

  • ½ cup unsalted butter
  • 4 oz semi-sweet chocolate (bar or chips)
  • 1 cup powdered sugar
  • 2 large eggs
  • 2 large egg yolks
  • 1 tsp vanilla extract
  • ½ cup all-purpose flour
  • Pinch of salt

Optional Toppings

  • Powdered sugar
  • Fresh strawberries
  • Vanilla ice cream

Instructions

  1. Preheat your oven to 425°F and lightly grease four ramekins or oven-safe dishes.
  2. Melt the butter and chocolate together in a microwave-safe bowl, heating in 30-second intervals and stirring until smooth.
  3. Whisk in powdered sugar until fully combined.
  4. Add eggs, egg yolks, and vanilla extract, whisking until the batter is glossy and smooth.
  5. Gently fold in flour and salt until just combined—avoid overmixing.
  6. Divide the batter evenly among the prepared ramekins and place them on a baking sheet.
  7. Bake for 12–14 minutes, until the edges are set but the centers remain soft and molten.
  8. Let cool for about one minute, then carefully invert onto plates—or enjoy warm right from the ramekin.

Warmth Worth Celebrating

Just like this lava cake, your home should always feel warm when it matters most.
